title: AI Breakout Capacity: A Middle-Power Path Between Racing and Dependence
gist: Leicht and Winter-Levy argue that frontier AI access is becoming scarce through security-restricted rollouts, compute shortages and U.S. export controls. Middle powers such as Germany, India and the UK should keep bargaining for imported frontier access, but they should also build a latent 'breakout' capacity to sprint to the frontier if they are cut off. That capacity means compute with guaranteed state access, champion firms kept alive as fast followers, emergency legal powers and decision reviews, all while staying aligned with the U.S. The authors estimate that a frontier training run needs only a low-single-digit share of global compute.

insights.claim: Three converging forces are making access to frontier AI scarce: security concerns lead developers to restrict new models to handpicked firms (as with Anthropic's restricted rollout of its cybersecurity model Mythos), compute shortages force usage limits, and the U.S. government is seeking control over how frontier systems reach the market, including export controls on Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Frontier model access is becoming a strategic, rationed good, which raises the pricing power of U.S. labs and the geopolitical value of compute.
insights.quote: Access to frontier AI may soon be rationed, conditioned, and switched on or off at the discretion of a handful of American firms and the government that oversees them.
insights.locator: Access to frontier artificial intelligence is becoming scarce

insights.claim: Anthropic's Project Glasswing managed-access policy showed that European governments and businesses expected serious cybersecurity vulnerabilities without access to the latest frontier model, and no European fast-follower model could ease those concerns.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Frontier capability is decisive in cyber defense, so being denied access creates real security exposure.
insights.locator: Project Glasswing, Anthropic’s managed access policy

insights.claim: Pure adoption or fast-follower strategies are failing because their enabling conditions are eroding. Followers once tracked the frontier at a six-to-nine-month lag through common techniques and distillation, but U.S. compute advantages are widening and may stay locked in for years, U.S. firms are cracking down on distillation, and revenue advantages may compound with automated AI R&D.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: The gap between frontier and sub-frontier models is likely to widen, which concentrates value in the leading U.S. labs and their compute suppliers.
insights.quote: Compute asymmetries between leading U.S. developers and the rest of the world are widening, and the gap may be locked in for at least the next several years
insights.locator: Until recently, that has been a reasonable bet

insights.claim: Frontier access will be decisive where relative capability matters: cyber defense against attackers using frontier systems, drug discovery and other scientific R&D where capability gaps decide market position, and military uses.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: These are the sectors where a middle power without frontier access is competitively exposed.
insights.locator: Middle powers can do many things with sub-frontier models

insights.claim: Sovereign frontier moonshots are out of reach even for middle-power alliances. Mistral raised at a valuation of about $14 billion in September 2025, while leading U.S. labs raise multiples of that per round and spend more than that on compute each year. Google alone controls roughly a quarter of the world's computing power.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Non-U.S. frontier challengers face a capital and compute gap of an order of magnitude; be skeptical of sovereign-AI valuations premised on reaching the frontier.
insights.locator: But strategically relevant capabilities are currently out of reach

insights.claim: The EU's planned AI 'gigafactory' compute hubs will at best match what U.S. companies built years ago when they come online.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Europe's public compute programs will not change the frontier balance.
insights.quote: When the EU’s planned gigafactories come online, they will at best match what U.S. companies built years ago.
insights.locator: But strategically relevant capabilities are currently out of reach

insights.claim: The politics of frontier moonshots are fraught: they need tens of billions of dollars upfront plus energy and grid allocations with no assured return, legacy industries will compete for cheap power, and divided publics will ask why data centers get priority over hospitals. These pressures already exist in the U.S. and will weigh more heavily in middle powers.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Expect political backlash over power and grid allocation to data centers, a constraint on AI infrastructure build-outs outside the U.S.
insights.locator: Right now, the politics of a frontier moonshot

insights.claim: Even a well-negotiated import deal cannot fully protect a middle power, because no contract written in advance can reliably stop a great power from cutting off frontier access for security, trade-leverage or political reasons. Middle powers can use critical minerals, data and advanced manufacturing as leverage, and add scaffolding that lets them shift workloads between providers.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Supports demand for multi-provider tooling and for sovereign-AI hedging spend by governments.
insights.locator: If neither building sovereign frontier models

themes.theme: The breakout posture: AI latency modeled on nuclear latency

insights.claim: The authors propose an 'AI breakout posture': stay aligned with a great-power patron and import frontier AI, while keeping the capacity to launch a frontier sprint if access deteriorates, modeled on Japan's tolerated nuclear latency. Unlike Ward-Jackson and McBride's 'good enough' sub-frontier fallback, the aim is a full catch-up to the frontier.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Gives a framework for reading middle-power AI policy, such as compute deals, emergency powers and national champions, as hedges rather than races.
insights.locator: The Breakout Posture

insights.claim: Delaying the sprint has four advantages over racing now. Financially, it hedges against an AI bubble or value shifting to small or specialized models. Politically, a short sprint under urgency is easier to sell than a years-long speculative project. Geopolitically, dependencies can be reduced before committing. Epistemically, it postpones betting on one technical paradigm.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Middle-power AI capex will probably be staged and option-like rather than all-in, which tempers expectations for sovereign AI spending.
insights.quote: Retaining the option of an AI sprint has four distinct advantages over attempting it immediately.
insights.locator: Retaining the option of such a sprint

insights.claim: A middle-power frontier project would probably get only one shot, since even an alliance could not fund several frontier players. The U.S. and China can avoid choosing a paradigm (reinforcement learning for coding, giant pre-training runs or efficient inference-heavy models) because they have many competing labs.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Single-champion sovereign AI bets carry high paradigm risk; the diversity of U.S. labs is a structural advantage.
insights.locator: The fourth is epistemic

insights.claim: Researchers estimate that under 10% of OpenAI's 2024 compute went to frontier training, so a breakout training run probably needs only a low-single-digit share of global compute. That is achievable for some middle powers or an alliance, though still beyond their projected capacity without concerted action.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Frontier training is a small slice of compute demand; inference and post-training dominate, which matters for the mix of AI infrastructure demand.
insights.locator: How much compute would be necessary

insights.claim: Middle powers can secure latent compute through state-owned build-outs (most reliable but most expensive), incentives for domestic private build-outs (likely too small), foreign hyperscalers and neoclouds hosted under compute-for-access deals, and long-term chip options with Nvidia and TSMC that are executed if needed or resold at a moderate loss.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Possible new demand channel for Nvidia and TSMC: government-underwritten long-term supply options from allies.
insights.locator: Fourth, countries can attempt to secure access

insights.claim: Host countries could negotiate latent access to foreign-owned data centers through Defense Production Act-style powers, general expropriation powers with above-market compensation, or narrow expropriation clauses that trigger only if operators revoke frontier access. Such terms would need offsetting build-out incentives such as energy price subsidies or guarantees.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: A new kind of sovereign risk for hyperscaler data centers abroad; watch for contingent expropriation clauses in host-country deals.
insights.locator: Possible measures along these lines might include

themes.theme: Champion firms, talent and coding-agent dependency

insights.claim: Only Mistral (France) and the Emirati state-backed G42 currently have the organizational capacity to attempt a frontier breakout; Canada's Cohere and Germany's Aleph Alpha could be developed into candidates.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: These firms are the likely vehicles for any sovereign-AI money if governments decide to sprint.
insights.locator: Today, the French company Mistral and the Emirati

insights.claim: Counterintuitively, governments should task their champion firms to stay deliberately behind the frontier as fast followers at a lag of about nine months, with guaranteed public-administration demand, rather than fund frontier development early and invite political backlash.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Sovereign AI champions may be steered toward government contracts at sub-frontier level, which caps their upside but supports their revenue floor.
insights.quote: Counterintuitively, middle-power governments should not prematurely employ these companies for frontier development itself
insights.locator: Today, the French company Mistral

insights.claim: Mistral's close ties to the French state would make other governments reluctant to put billions into it as a coalition breakout vehicle without complex governance commitments.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Single-nation champions face governance hurdles in attracting pan-European funding.
insights.locator: A latent breakout project would also require standing

insights.claim: Distillation of U.S. frontier models is a fragile basis for middle powers: it partly explains the success of Chinese open-source models, but U.S. developers and the government could impose much stricter API access rules if they felt threatened. Antagonizing the U.S. would also endanger the chip imports a breakout depends on.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Tighter API and distillation restrictions are a risk for open-source model developers that rely on distillation.
insights.locator: As they build that capacity, middle powers would be wise

insights.claim: Much of the software engineering at frontier labs is already done by internal coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex, and labs increasingly restrict competitors' use of their models. If this continues, a breakout project could be unable to catch up for lack of AI coding capability, which could force governments to launch immediately or give up.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Access to coding agents is becoming a strategic chokepoint, strengthening the moat of leading labs.
insights.locator: The final necessary element

insights.claim: Retaining talent requires prestige employers able to host sensitive work, such as DeepMind in London and Anthropic's and OpenAI's growing European offices, together with education pipelines, since neither retention nor training works alone against the richest firms' hiring sprees.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Supports policies that court U.S. lab offices in Europe; the talent war favors deep-pocketed U.S. firms.
insights.locator: The first is talent

themes.theme: State capacity, coalition design and U.S. tolerance

insights.claim: Governments need emergency legal powers in advance to redirect national energy, consolidate compute and talent, and compel firms, such as the U.S. Defense Production Act, France's Code de la défense and Canada's Defence Production Act. They should also run regular reviews of whether the frontier gap is widening, whether access deals are fraying, whether suppliers are using access as leverage, and whether automated AI R&D is speeding up abroad.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: These review questions double as investor signposts for when AI access becomes geopolitically contested.
insights.locator: The second requirement is the institutional capacity

insights.claim: A coalition breakout could in principle run French or Canadian models on British-designed chips, funded by Norwegian sovereign wealth and hosted in Finland. Coordination costs are huge, so the authors recommend building national capabilities first with hooks for later consolidation.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Expect national-first sovereign AI programs with loose interoperability rather than a single EU frontier lab.
insights.locator: A breakout posture could be mounted

insights.claim: History offers two templates: India absorbed years of U.S. sanctions and eventually won acceptance of its nuclear status in the 2008 deal, while Iran, visible enough to provoke intervention but too weak to deter it, suffered sanctions, cyberattacks, assassinations and strikes. A breakout candidate should therefore stay strongly aligned with the U.S., which controls a prohibitive chip-supply bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Middle-power AI hedging will stay within the U.S. stack, which reinforces U.S. chip and cloud dominance rather than fragmenting it.
insights.quote: given the current structure of the chip supply chain, the United States simply controls a prohibitive bottleneck
insights.locator: Some of this has to do with posture

insights.claim: The more reliably the U.S. supplies frontier AI to allies, the less reason they have to launch a breakout. Allies who feel trapped are the ones most likely to turn to Chinese offers or costly moonshots that fragment the U.S.-led AI ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Unreliable U.S. AI export policy would speed fragmentation and boost sovereign-AI and Chinese alternatives.
insights.quote: Washington should make itself the kind of supplier that makes a breakout sprint unnecessary.
insights.locator: U.S. policymakers, for their part

insights.claim: Betting everything on the U.S. remaining a stable, benign AI supplier would be 'geopolitical malpractice', but so would overconfidence that middle powers can catch up now or safely take a hostile stance toward U.S. AI firms.
insights.speaker: Anton Leicht
insights.so_what: Middle-power policy will mix deep U.S. integration with quiet sovereign hedging, so allied demand for U.S. AI should hold up.
insights.quote: But placing every chip on that bet would be geopolitical malpractice.
insights.locator: A latent breakout capacity can help middle powers
